video_title: Inside the $1.2 Billion Endowment Playbook ft. Paul Chai | Allocator | Ep. 36
gist: Paul Chai, CIO of the $1.2bn Kansas State University Foundation endowment, walks through a 60/40 portfolio in which the 40% is deliberately not bonds — because he doubts bonds still hedge equities — and is instead diversifier hedge funds, real assets, private credit and a liquidity sleeve. His edge case is buying where capital is leaving for non-economic reasons: he added to traditional oil and gas as large LPs stopped re-upping, and has been a net buyer of private-asset secondaries as endowment-tax uncertainty and research-budget pressure forced bigger institutions to raise liquidity. He also discloses that his newly adopted allocation only carries a 51–52% modeled probability of hitting its 6% real / 8% nominal target, runs no CTA allocation today because trend and momentum have commoditized, and screens managers on 'grit' — harmonious versus obsessive passion — rather than pedigree.

insights.claim: Kansas State University Foundation frames its $1.2bn endowment as a 'forever retiree' — needing dependable income, inflation protection and growth, but with an infinite planning horizon — which pushes the portfolio toward consistent compounding rather than any single strong year.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: The mandate framing explains why this class of buyer will keep bidding for illiquid, long-duration assets through drawdowns rather than de-risking with the crowd.
insights.quote: we manage the endowment as if the endowment is a forever retiree

insights.claim: The foundation's stated long-term objective is roughly 6% real return net of inflation, or about 8% nominal, and it explicitly aims for 'singles and doubles' rather than home runs in any single year.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: An 8% nominal hurdle from a patient pool of capital sets the return bar any manager pitching this LP segment must clear net of fees.
insights.quote: We're not trying to hit a home run in any single year. We're trying to consistently hit singles and doubles to compound capital, support annual spending and preserve purchasing power across generations.

insights.claim: Chai deliberately rejected optimizing the strategic asset allocation for a single objective, instead building separate optimized portfolios for maximum return, probability of hitting the real target, liquidity risk, spending-decline risk and drawdown risk, then selecting the mix that ranked in the upper half on every dimension rather than first on one.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A robustness-across-scenarios selection rule, rather than mean-variance maximization, is what actually determines allocation flows from this LP cohort.
insights.quote: choosing an allocation uh that wins in more than one version uh of the future

insights.claim: Running a thousand Monte Carlo scenarios, each with its own economic conditions and resulting inflation, the foundation's adopted portfolio shows only a roughly 51–52% probability of achieving its long-term real return objective over the next 10 years.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A sophisticated allocator admitting roughly coin-flip odds on an 8% nominal target is a candid signal that forward return expectations across mainstream asset classes are thin.
insights.quote: we are looking at potentially uh achieving our long-term return objective um at about 51 to 52%. So it's it's not it's not going to be a high certainty but it's better than half.

insights.claim: The foundation imposes implementability guardrails on its strategic asset allocation — limits around liquidity, private market exposure, commitment pacing and existing commitments — so any new target can realistically be reached within two to three years, plus a transition plan and a fair benchmarking framework so the team is not judged on exposures it has not yet been able to change.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Explains why large allocation shifts by endowments arrive as multi-year commitment flows rather than immediate portfolio turnover.
insights.quote: a strategic asset allocation is not useful if we propose a new target that cannot be implemented uh before we run the next study

themes.theme: 60/40 Rebuilt With Illiquidity Instead of Bonds

insights.claim: The endowment runs a 60/40 shape where the 60% growth bucket is all equity-related risk, split roughly 55% public equity and 45% private equity.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A near-half private weighting inside the growth sleeve means this LP's equity beta is structurally locked up and slow to reprice.

insights.claim: Chai is skeptical that bonds can still hedge equity volatility given the changed stock-bond correlation, and would rather use his ability to hold less liquid assets than rely on fixed income as the diversifier.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: If long-horizon institutions structurally substitute illiquid diversifiers for duration, marginal demand for long bonds from this buyer base is weaker than history implies.
insights.quote: we tend to be a little bit skeptical about bonds ability to hedge stock market volatility and we think we can do better uh by having more flexibility to take on less liquid assets

insights.claim: The non-equity 40% is deliberately not a bond portfolio: it comprises a dedicated liquidity sleeve sized to fund campus distributions and private capital calls, plus diversifier hedge funds, real assets (infrastructure, energy, real estate) and private credit, each expected to deliver low-to-negative correlation to equities.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Maps exactly where endowment dollars displaced from fixed income are going — a demand tailwind for private credit, real assets and diversifying hedge strategies.

insights.claim: Chai argues the sweet spot for an allocator is running under about $5 billion — big enough to be an important partner to managers, small enough that the portfolio's footprint is not noticeable to the market and idiosyncratic positions can still move the needle.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Implies capacity-constrained, niche strategies are best sold to sub-$5bn pools, while multi-billion allocators are structurally pushed into liquid beta.
insights.quote: I tend to think that if you're managing a portfolio uh that's less than $5 billion you're probably in a pretty sweet spot

themes.theme: Poor Man's Total Portfolio Approach & Liquid Hurdles

insights.claim: With a four-person investment team plus students, Chai runs what he calls a 'poor man's total portfolio approach': every private investment must clear a conviction bar of outperforming an available public equivalent strategy before it earns a place.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A replicable discipline for any allocator: price the illiquidity premium against a live public alternative rather than against a private-market benchmark.
insights.quote: I I call it the poor man's total portfolio approach

insights.claim: The foundation deliberately places niche public-market strategies inside its private credit and private equity buckets so they function as liquid hurdles that anything illiquid must beat.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Managers raising illiquid vehicles should expect to be benchmarked against liquid substitutes held in the same bucket, compressing tolerance for weak private premia.

insights.claim: Within private credit the foundation holds structured credit plus credit dislocation strategies that invest in public credit and target short-term returns of 20%-plus IRR when valuations in structured or other public credit sectors dislocate.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Identifies dry powder waiting to buy public credit dislocations — a marginal bid that caps how far certain credit sectors widen.
insights.quote: have a give you a case where you can get a short-term return of 20% plus irr and uh the strategies take advantage of these dislocations

insights.claim: Chai argues the structural failure mode of strategic asset allocation at large institutions is that big siloed teams create local optimization, where asset-class heads push to grow their own allocation partly because their bonus is aligned to it.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A governance lens for reading big-institution allocation shifts: some flows reflect internal incentives, not conviction, and can be faded.
insights.quote: sometimes you have local optimization where each asset class heads are trying to optimize their performance

insights.claim: Chai says the popular reading of David Swenson's work — own less traditional fixed income and more hedge funds, private equity, venture and real assets — misses the deeper lesson, which is that long-term investors should hunt less trafficked, less transparent and less efficiently priced markets only where they have the governance, patience, access and skill to do so.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Reframes the endowment model as a capability test rather than an asset-label test, implying copycat allocators without those capabilities will underperform the template.
insights.quote: Complexity is not an asset class and eli liquidity is not automatically alpha.

insights.claim: Before committing to any unconventional exposure Chai runs a four-question test: what role the asset class plays, where the market is inefficient, whether that inefficiency should persist, and what capability is required to capture it — plus whether the investor is actually paid for the added complexity, illiquidity or active risk.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A concrete diligence checklist for judging whether an alternative allocation is compensated or just complicated.

insights.claim: The foundation caps unconventionality with an explicit risk budget on deviation from its benchmark, aiming to be unconventional only where there is a compelling reason to believe the opportunity is real rather than across the whole book.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Explains why even conviction-driven endowments size idiosyncratic bets modestly — position sizing is constrained by tracking-error budget, not just view strength.
insights.quote: the goal is to be unconventional where we have a compelling reason to believe that opportunity is real

insights.claim: Chai's core opportunity screen is capital leaving an asset class for non-economic reasons — when large institutions stop committing or are forced to sell for governance, tax or liquidity reasons rather than investment merit, he treats the opportunity as more compelling, not less.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A repeatable sourcing rule: track forced or policy-driven outflows as the entry signal, independent of fundamentals.
insights.quote: whenever you have outflows of capital out out of a certain asset class and and it's for reasons that that's not economic um then then those are those become something that that we look at and we become interested in

insights.claim: The foundation increased its allocation to traditional oil and gas in private real assets roughly two to three years ago after learning at energy partners' annual meetings that large institutions were declining to re-commit for governance and other non-economic reasons rather than weak investment opportunity.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Confirms an LP-level supply/demand imbalance in traditional energy funds that boosts terms and pricing for the allocators still willing to commit.

insights.claim: The endowment has been a net buyer in private-asset secondary markets over the last two years as larger institutions were forced sellers of higher-quality private assets, driven by endowment tax uncertainty, government restrictions on research budgets that pushed universities to tap endowments for liquidity, and impatient retail and employee holders of late-stage private tech shares willing to sell at a discount.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Names the specific policy and liquidity catalysts creating discounted secondary supply — a window that closes if the endowment tax and research funding picture resolves.
insights.quote: we we had been a net buyer in the secondary markets over the last two years when um larger institutions are forced to sell some of their higher quality private assets

insights.claim: In traditional energy the foundation chose to weight commitments toward equity rather than debt after comparing upside against downside risk across the capital structure, though it did also make a credit commitment.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Capital-structure selection, not just sector selection, drove the outcome — a reminder that the same non-economic-seller thesis can pay in equity and fail in credit.

insights.claim: Chai concedes the energy credit investment has not worked out well because financing conditions for traditional energy improved while public energy companies practiced fiscal discipline and refused to lever up, so returning banks and lenders competed away the opportunity.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A live warning that private energy lending spreads are being compressed by bank re-entry plus weak borrower demand — underwrite energy credit accordingly.
insights.quote: the the credit investment in traditional energy actually hasn't worked out too well for us

themes.theme: Hedge Fund Barbell, Pod Shops & Fee Philosophy

insights.claim: The diversifier hedge fund bucket is underwritten to deliver the same 8% nominal / 6%-plus real return as the rest of the portfolio but with zero-to-negative correlation, using arbitrage and volatility strategies that trade short-term deltas and volatility rather than buy-and-hold growth.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Sets the bar for pitching this LP: diversification alone is not enough, the return stream must also clear 8% nominal.

insights.claim: The hedge fund sleeve is structured as an internal barbell: an absolute-return portion targeted above 8% specifically to pay for a smaller higher-convexity sleeve that acts as a put option on the portfolio and is expected to lose money in calm periods.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Shows how institutions actually finance tail protection — the carry cost is explicitly budgeted against a higher-return sleeve, which is what makes long-vol allocations survivable.
insights.quote: these are more of a insurance type of strategies that that will essentially create a put option to to the portfolio uh which which will cost you

insights.claim: Chai holds multi-strategy pod shops and says the best of them historically offer everything an allocator wants — above-8% absolute returns, high Sharpe, stable and low-correlated streams — with his main reservation being periods of heavy market crowding rather than the fees.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Crowding, not fee level, is the risk institutional LPs are actually monitoring in multi-strats — watch position-crowding unwinds as the trigger for redemptions.
insights.quote: I think the part that we tend to be a little bit more concerned are periods when you have a lot of market crowding.

insights.claim: Chai is explicitly willing to pay high multi-strat fees, deciding fee tolerance by measuring the return dispersion between top-quartile and bottom-quartile managers in each asset class — wide dispersion justifies paying up, while treasuries and liquidity buckets should be passive or self-managed.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A clean rule for where fee compression will and will not bite: dispersion, not headline cost, determines which managers keep pricing power.
insights.quote: you probably do not want to pay high fees to a active manager to manage your treasury allocation

insights.claim: The foundation currently has no CTA allocation despite having held them in the past, because classic trend, momentum and reversal return drivers have become commoditized and cheaply replicable, while less conventional managed futures programs behave as black boxes that are hard to underwrite through regime changes.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A direct headwind for traditional CTA fundraising from endowments — replication at lower cost is now the default alternative.
insights.quote: some some of these investment return drivers have become more commoditized and that that's where you can nowadays replicate some of these um return factors on your own with with lower cost

insights.claim: For the complexity/protection side of the book Chai underwrites strategies against a specific named risk — tight interest spreads, currency risk, or an inflation spike or significant credit spread widening — rather than buying generic diversification.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Hedges are bought against identified scenarios with predictable payoffs, which is the standard a protection strategy must meet to win institutional capital.

insights.claim: Chai refuses to start manager diligence with a bias toward established or emerging managers, arguing established firms offer resources and stability while emerging ones offer alignment, focus and less crowded opportunities — but neither label is itself an investment thesis.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Emerging managers can access this LP cohort without a brand-name pedigree if the opportunity and strategy fit come first.
insights.quote: I try not to confuse pedigree with capability

insights.claim: The foundation's manager selection follows a fixed sequence — the opportunity must fit the portfolio, the strategy must fit the opportunity, and only then are the people assessed for partnership fit.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Inbound pitches are screened top-down against allocation need first, so timing a pitch to an LP's transition period matters more than manager quality alone.

insights.claim: Chai argues allocators should deliberately act on roughly 60–70% of the information rather than chasing certainty, because by the time 100% of the information on an opportunity is collected the opportunity has sailed or is already fully priced.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Codifies the information-versus-timing tradeoff — excess diligence is itself a source of underperformance for allocators.
insights.quote: by the time you collect your 100% of information about a certain certain investment opportunity um chances are your investment opportunity has already sailed

insights.claim: Chai treats grit — decomposed into passion plus perseverance — as one of the biggest predictors of a manager's future success, and weights it most heavily for emerging managers who lack a five- or ten-year track record that can be modeled in a spreadsheet.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: For track-record-light managers, qualitative resilience assessment is the actual gate to institutional capital.
insights.quote: grit can be decomposed as passion plus perseverance

insights.claim: Chai distinguishes harmonious passion — curiosity and purpose serving a greater good — from obsessive passion focused on self at any cost, and avoids the latter because obsessive-passion managers get frustrated more easily and can break down when things do not go their way, probing how candidates handled adversity to tell the two apart.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A behavioral filter that predicts which managers blow up or quit in a drawdown — applicable to hiring and to fund diligence alike.
insights.quote: people who have obsessive passion tend to be um less healthy. They they can potentially run into problems when things don't go their way.

insights.claim: Chai argues portfolios are reflections of the people who built them, and says reviewing inherited Kansas State managers taught him about the preferences of the prior decision makers — his own bias being sympathy for underdogs and outsiders breaking into the industry.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Portfolio archaeology is a practical diligence tool: reading an existing book reveals the decision maker's systematic tilts before you inherit or underwrite them.
insights.quote: our portfolios are all reflections of parts of ourselves

insights.claim: Kansas State's investment team operates on consensus: a single strong objection from any one of its six members blocks an investment, and Chai says he will respect that veto even as CIO — a rule he concedes might not work on a larger team.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: A one-person veto structurally biases a small allocator toward fewer, higher-conviction commitments and against consensus-breaking bets.
insights.quote: If there is even one out of the the six members on my team that have a strong opposition to a investment we we want to make even a CIO I I will respect that that opinion and we will not make the investment.

insights.claim: Chai learned that his engineer's instinct for exhaustive, technical board reporting actively discouraged non-investment board members from participating, and now optimizes board communication for clarity of direction over completeness and data accuracy.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Governance quality depends on board engagement, and over-technical reporting is a concrete way institutions lose the challenge function that protects the portfolio.
insights.quote: learning how to explain things in a way that uh is more about clarity of direction as opposed to the completeness and the accuracy of the data

insights.claim: The foundation runs an annual process collecting and presenting all manager fees and team operating expenses to its investment committee after each fiscal year end, which Chai calls a point of pride given the team's small size.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Institutionalized fee transparency to the committee means fee discussions with this LP are evidence-based and recurring, not one-off negotiations.

insights.claim: Chai says the CIO role is much broader than picking investments — the real responsibility is building a durable decision-making system combining clear mission, governance, a strong team, a disciplined process and the willingness to act when evidence changes, which is why he has spent three years deliberately hiring people who think differently from him.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: Judge an institutional allocator on its decision system and team diversity, not on any single manager pick or year of returns.
insights.quote: the real responsibility is to build a durable decision making system

insights.claim: Chai's closing advice for long-horizon investors is to counter the industry's default fast-thinking pattern recognition with slower, deliberate analysis and humility, invoking Ted Lasso's 'be curious, not judgmental' and Daniel Kahneman's Thinking Fast and Slow.
insights.speaker: Paul Chai
insights.so_what: The structural advantage of permanent capital is permission to think slowly — a discipline shorter-horizon investors cannot replicate.
insights.quote: you want to be curious and not not to be judgmental
